title: Mental Models and Reality Testing
subtitle: The Map Is Not the Territory
description: Learn to recognize when your mental models diverge from reality and how to update them based on evidence.
learningObjectives: Understand what mental models are and how they shape perception

content.overview: Mental models are the internal representations we use to understand the world. They are simplified frameworks that help us interpret information, make predictions, and decide on actions. In government digital transformation, the mental models held by leaders, technical teams, and citizens fundamentally shape what's possible.

keyPoints.title: What Mental Models Are
characteristics: Built from experience, education, and culture
Enable rapid decision-making by reducing complexity
examples: A ministry official's model of 'how government IT projects work'
A citizen's model of 'what happens when I apply for a permit'
A vendor's model of 'what government clients want'
A donor's model of 'how developing countries adopt technology'
keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: Every stakeholder in DPI implementation carries mental models about technology, bureaucracy, citizens, and change - these models drive their behavior more than formal policies do

formationSources.description: Personal encounters with systems, successes, and failures
formationSources.example: An IT director who experienced a failed ERP implementation will have a different model of 'big IT projects' than one who hasn't
formationSources.implication: People with different experiences literally see different realities

formationSources.description: Shared narratives and assumptions within organizations
formationSources.example: A ministry with a history of donor-driven projects may model 'digital transformation' as 'external intervention' rather than 'internal capability building'
formationSources.implication: Organizational mental models persist even when individuals change

formationSources.example: Engineers model problems differently than administrators; economists see different patterns than sociologists
formationSources.implication: Professional training creates predictable blind spots alongside expertise

formationSources.description: Stories that shape understanding of unfamiliar domains
formationSources.example: Coverage of 'digital government success in Estonia' shapes mental models even for those who've never visited
formationSources.implication: Vivid stories can create strong but potentially inaccurate models

keyPoints.title: Why Mental Models Matter for DPI

reasons.example: A leader whose model says 'citizens distrust government apps' won't notice evidence of successful adoption

reasons.reason: They shape interpretation of ambiguous events
reasons.example: Low initial usage of a digital payment system: is it 'failed adoption' or 'normal learning curve'? Depends on your model
If your model is 'government can't build good software,' you'll only consider vendor solutions

reasons.reason: They determine what seems risky vs safe
reasons.example: Building in-house seems risky to some models, outsourcing seems risky to others

content.keyInsight: Mental models are not optional - everyone has them. The question is whether your models are accurate enough for your decisions, and whether you know where they might be wrong.

exercises.prompt: Write down your mental model of 'how digital identity systems succeed or fail.' What experiences formed this model? What assumptions are you making that you haven't tested?

content.overview: Mental models don't just organize information - they actively filter and transform it. You literally see different things depending on your models. This has profound implications for collaboration across different stakeholder groups in DPI implementation.

mechanisms.description: Models direct what we notice and ignore
mechanisms.example: A security-focused model notices vulnerabilities; a user-experience model notices friction points. Same system, different observations.
mechanisms.inDPIContext: Technical teams and policy teams literally see different aspects of the same digital identity system

mechanisms.description: Models fill in missing information with expectations
mechanisms.example: When a vendor is late on a deliverable, some models complete the pattern as 'they're struggling' while others complete it as 'they're incompetent'
mechanisms.inDPIContext: Initial impressions get amplified because we fill gaps with model-consistent assumptions

mechanisms.description: Model-consistent information is easily absorbed; inconsistent information requires extra processing
mechanisms.example: If your model says 'this project will fail,' success metrics feel like exceptions needing explanation while failures feel like confirmation
mechanisms.inDPIContext: Skeptics and champions can look at the same data and reach opposite conclusions

interpretationEffects.description: Models provide ready-made explanations for events
interpretationEffects.governmentExample: Digital payment pilot fails. Attribution depends on model: 'Users not ready' (citizen model) vs 'Poor design' (technical model) vs 'Insufficient political support' (institutional model)
interpretationEffects.consequence: Different attributions lead to completely different responses

interpretationEffects.description: Models determine what events mean and how important they are
interpretationEffects.governmentExample: One minister champions DPI publicly. Some models: 'Finally, political will!' Others: 'Just another announcement, wait for action'
interpretationEffects.consequence: Same event can trigger mobilization or cynicism depending on models

interpretationEffects.description: Models suggest what past experiences are relevant
interpretationEffects.governmentExample: New digital identity proposal. Some see analogy to successful national ID card. Others see analogy to failed biometric voting system. Different analogies, different expectations.
interpretationEffects.consequence: The analogies your model suggests determine what lessons you apply

challenges.description: When mental models differ, the same words mean different things
challenges.example: 'Interoperability' means technical API compatibility to engineers, data sharing agreements to lawyers, and cross-ministry coordination to administrators
challenges.solution: Explicitly surface what terms mean to different stakeholders

challenges.description: Surface agreement can mask deep model differences
challenges.example: Everyone agrees 'citizen privacy is important' but models differ on what that requires in practice
challenges.solution: Probe with specific scenarios to reveal model differences

challenges.description: Different models accept different evidence as valid
challenges.example: Technologist wants pilot data; minister wants political feasibility analysis; donor wants theory of change. Each model privileges different proof.
challenges.solution: Understand what evidence each stakeholder's model requires

content.keyInsight: When stakeholders disagree, it's often not that they have different values or intelligence - they literally perceive different realities through different mental models. Effective DPI leadership requires understanding and bridging these perceptual gaps.

exercises.prompt: Choose a current DPI initiative. Describe it from three different stakeholder perspectives (e.g., citizen, IT department, minister). What does each stakeholder 'see' that the others miss? What do they interpret differently?

modules.title: Common Faulty Mental Models in Government

content.overview: Certain mental models recur across government digital transformation efforts. Some are partially true but dangerously incomplete. Others are outdated remnants from previous eras. Recognizing these common faulty models helps you avoid their traps.

faultyModels.belief: If we just implement the right technology, everything else will follow
faultyModels.whyItPersists: Technology is tangible and can be purchased, unlike organizational change
faultyModels.reality: Technology amplifies existing capabilities and dysfunctions. Without institutional change, new technology often creates new problems.
faultyModels.betterModel: Technology as enabler that requires complementary institutional, process, and capability changes
faultyModels.dpiExample: Digital identity system implemented without updating registration processes, leading to massive backlogs at enrollment centers

faultyModels.belief: What worked in India/Estonia/Singapore will work here
faultyModels.whyItPersists: Success stories are compelling and provide seemingly proven blueprints
faultyModels.reality: Context differences (institutional capacity, connectivity, literacy, political economy) mean the same technical solution produces different outcomes
faultyModels.betterModel: Learn principles from success stories, but adapt to local context through iterative testing
faultyModels.dpiExample: Aadhaar-style biometric system fails in context with unreliable electricity and limited enrollment infrastructure

faultyModels.model: Build It and They Will Come
faultyModels.belief: If we create a good digital service, citizens will naturally adopt it
faultyModels.whyItPersists: Technologists focus on technical quality; consumer tech creates expectation of natural virality
faultyModels.reality: Government services compete with established paper processes, require behavior change, and serve populations with varying digital access
faultyModels.betterModel: Adoption requires deliberate strategy: incentives, mandates, trust-building, channel migration planning
faultyModels.dpiExample: Excellent digital permit system sits unused because paper process remains easier and more trusted

faultyModels.belief: Real innovation only happens in private sector; government should buy, not build
faultyModels.whyItPersists: High-profile government IT failures; private sector innovation narratives
faultyModels.reality: Governments have driven major innovations (internet, GPS); capability varies widely; some functions require government ownership
faultyModels.betterModel: Government innovation is possible but requires different approaches than private sector
faultyModels.dpiExample: Country outsources entire DPI stack to vendor, loses strategic capability and becomes locked-in

faultyModels.belief: Nothing happens without minister/president ordering it
faultyModels.whyItPersists: Hierarchical culture; visible examples of political-will-driven change
faultyModels.reality: Top-down mandates without middle management buy-in often fail; bottom-up changes can scale; hybrid approaches often work best
faultyModels.betterModel: Effective change usually requires alignment across levels, not just top-down or bottom-up
faultyModels.dpiExample: President announces digital transformation, but implementation fails because mid-level bureaucrats weren't engaged in design

faultyModels.belief: If we mandate digital, people will comply and the old way will disappear
faultyModels.whyItPersists: Government has coercive power; mandates are administratively simple
faultyModels.reality: Mandates create parallel systems, workarounds, and resistance when underlying issues aren't addressed
faultyModels.betterModel: Mandates work when the digital option is genuinely better and accessible; otherwise they create gaming
faultyModels.dpiExample: Digital-only business registration creates black market for 'helpers' who navigate system for those who can't

faultyModels.belief: Digital transformation fails because citizens are uneducated/resistant/prefer corruption
faultyModels.whyItPersists: Easier to blame users than examine system design; some resistance does exist
faultyModels.reality: Citizens are rational actors responding to incentives and constraints; 'resistance' often signals design problems
faultyModels.betterModel: Citizen behavior is feedback about system design; resistance is information, not obstacle
faultyModels.dpiExample: Low digital payment adoption blamed on 'cash culture' when actual barrier was unreliable network coverage

faultyModels.belief: Opposition to digital transformation is about protecting turf/corruption/status quo
faultyModels.whyItPersists: Political resistance does exist; it's a convenient explanation for failure
faultyModels.reality: Legitimate concerns often underlie resistance: job security, workload, capability gaps, genuine risks
faultyModels.betterModel: Resistance has multiple sources; addressing legitimate concerns often neutralizes political opposition
faultyModels.dpiExample: Ministry opposition framed as 'protecting fiefdom' when actual concern was lack of capacity for new responsibilities

faultyModels.belief: If people aren't using the system correctly, they need more training
faultyModels.whyItPersists: Training is a concrete, purchasable intervention; it addresses visible symptoms
faultyModels.reality: Poor usage often reflects system design, incentives, or organizational issues that training can't fix
faultyModels.betterModel: Training works when capability is the actual gap; other interventions needed for design/incentive/organizational issues
faultyModels.dpiExample: Repeated training programs for government staff who still use workarounds because system doesn't fit their actual workflow

content.keyInsight: These faulty models aren't stupid - they each contain partial truth. The problem is treating partial models as complete, or applying models from one context to another where they don't fit. Always ask: 'What is this model missing?'

exercises.prompt: Identify a DPI initiative that struggled or failed. Which of the faulty mental models above contributed to the problems? What would a better model have suggested doing differently?

content.overview: Alfred Korzybski's insight that 'the map is not the territory' is foundational for clear thinking. All mental models are maps - useful abstractions that are necessarily incomplete. Confusion arises when we mistake our maps for reality itself.

concepts.description: Reality itself - infinitely complex, constantly changing, directly experienced
examples: The actual behavior of citizens using a digital service
The real technical capabilities and limitations of a system
The genuine motivations and constraints of a ministry official
The actual flow of a government process in practice

concepts.description: Our mental representation of reality - simplified, static, abstracted
examples: User personas and journey maps
System architecture diagrams
Stakeholder analysis frameworks
Process flow documentation

concepts.description: Treating the map as if it were the territory
examples: Believing the org chart describes how decisions actually get made
Assuming the requirements document captures what users actually need
Thinking the project plan reflects how implementation will actually unfold
Treating the success metrics as the actual goals rather than proxies
concepts.consequences: Plans that don't survive contact with reality; surprises that 'should have been obvious'; inability to learn from feedback

keyPoints.title: Levels of Abstraction

levels.example: Watching a citizen attempt to enroll in digital ID at a registration center
levels.weaknesses: Time-consuming, hard to generalize, can't scale

levels.example: Field report documenting common enrollment problems
Taxonomy of enrollment barriers: technical, procedural, behavioral
levels.weaknesses: Categories may not fit reality; framework becomes the lens

levels.example: Model of digital service adoption in low-connectivity contexts
levels.weaknesses: Very far from ground reality; easy to mistake model for truth

keyPoints.guideline: The higher the abstraction level, the more useful for planning and the more dangerous if treated as reality. Regularly return to ground level to test abstractions.

practices.example: Instead of 'Users don't trust the system' (interpretation), say 'Usage dropped 40% after the security incident' (observation)
practices.benefit: Separates what you actually know from what you're inferring

practices.description: Know where your information comes from and how many times it's been abstracted
practices.example: 'The minister said X' vs 'I heard that someone in the ministry thinks X' - very different reliability
practices.benefit: Calibrates confidence appropriately to information quality

practices.description: Periodically return to direct observation to test your maps
practices.example: Even as a senior official, occasionally observe actual citizen interactions, not just reports about them
practices.benefit: Catches map drift before it causes major errors

practices.description: Maintain multiple maps of the same territory
practices.example: Technical architecture diagram AND process flow diagram AND stakeholder map - each captures different aspects
practices.benefit: Reduces blind spots from any single map's limitations

content.keyInsight: The map-territory distinction is not about maps being bad - they're essential. It's about maintaining awareness that your map is not reality, so you stay open to signals that your map needs updating.

exercises.prompt: Take a key planning document you use (stakeholder map, project plan, user personas). At what abstraction level is it? When did you last ground-truth it against direct observation? What might your map be missing?

content.overview: Your mental models will inevitably drift from reality. The skill is not having perfect models but recognizing quickly when models need updating. This module covers the signals that indicate model-reality mismatch and how to create feedback loops that surface them.

signals.description: When outcomes repeatedly differ from expectations in similar ways
examples: Projects consistently take longer than planned
Stakeholder reactions repeatedly surprise you
User behavior doesn't match your personas
signals.interpretation: Your model is systematically wrong about something - the pattern of surprises reveals what
signals.governmentContext: If every ministry engagement is 'unexpectedly' difficult, your model of ministry dynamics needs updating

signals.description: When you find yourself generating explanations for why contradicting evidence doesn't count
examples: 'That pilot success was a special case'
'The negative feedback is from people who don't understand'
'Those metrics don't capture what really matters'
signals.interpretation: Your model is probably wrong and you're protecting it from disconfirmation
signals.governmentContext: If you're dismissing all criticism of a DPI approach, ask whether your model might be the problem

signals.description: When smart, well-intentioned people consistently misunderstand you or you them
examples: Technical explanations that confuse rather than clarify
Recommendations that get implemented 'wrong'
Agreements that unravel because parties meant different things
signals.interpretation: Different mental models are creating different interpretations of the same words
signals.governmentContext: If ministry partners repeatedly 'misunderstand' requirements, your model of their understanding is wrong

signals.description: When your forecasts about what will happen are consistently inaccurate
examples: Adoption curves that don't match projections
Political dynamics that evolve differently than expected
Technical challenges that weren't anticipated
signals.interpretation: Your model of how the system works is wrong in ways that matter
signals.governmentContext: If your DPI rollout timeline is always wrong, your model of government implementation speed needs work

signals.description: When you realize nothing could convince you your model is wrong
examples: 'If it succeeds, the approach was right; if it fails, implementation was poor'
'Either way, this proves we need more of X'
Every outcome confirms the model
signals.interpretation: Your model has become a belief system rather than a testable framework
signals.governmentContext: If your theory of change can't be wrong, it's not useful for learning

feedbackTypes.implementation: Schedule periodic field visits; attend citizen service interactions; observe system usage
feedbackTypes.governmentApplication: Even senior DPI advisors should occasionally watch enrollment, payments, or service delivery in person
feedbackTypes.frequency: Monthly for active projects; quarterly for monitoring

feedbackTypes.description: Get input from multiple perspectives, especially those who disagree with you
feedbackTypes.implementation: Build relationships with skeptics; create safe channels for bad news; actively solicit criticism
feedbackTypes.governmentApplication: Include ministry critics, not just champions, in feedback loops; listen to frontline staff, not just managers

feedbackTypes.description: Measure what matters and watch for deviations from expectations
feedbackTypes.implementation: Define expected metrics before launch; track actuals vs expected; investigate significant deviations
feedbackTypes.governmentApplication: Track adoption rates, error rates, processing times against your model's predictions
feedbackTypes.frequency: Continuous monitoring with periodic deep-dive analysis

feedbackTypes.description: Regularly review what you expected vs what happened
feedbackTypes.implementation: Document predictions before decisions; review outcomes explicitly; identify model updates needed
feedbackTypes.governmentApplication: After each project phase, compare what you thought would happen vs what did
feedbackTypes.frequency: After major milestones; quarterly for ongoing work

debuggingProcess.description: What specific outcome violated your expectations?
questions: What did you expect to happen?

debuggingProcess.description: What beliefs led to your expectation?
questions: Where did those assumptions come from?

debuggingProcess.description: What other models could explain the outcome?
questions: What would have to be true for this outcome to happen?
What model would have predicted this?

debuggingProcess.description: What evidence would distinguish between models?
questions: What would each model predict for future observations?
What data would you need to collect?

content.keyInsight: The goal is not to have a model that's never wrong - that's impossible. The goal is to detect wrongness quickly so you can update before errors compound. Build systems that surface model failures rather than hide them.

exercises.prompt: Map the feedback loops in a current project. Where do you get information about reality? Who tells you when things aren't working? What signals would indicate your model is wrong, and would you actually receive those signals?

content.overview: Recognizing that your model needs updating is only half the challenge. The other half is actually updating it - rationally, based on evidence, rather than swinging to the opposite extreme or getting stuck. This module introduces principles of evidence-based belief revision.

principles.description: Change your confidence in proportion to the strength of evidence
principles.badPattern: All-or-nothing: 'One failure proves the whole approach is wrong'
principles.goodPattern: Graduated: 'This failure reduces my confidence from 80% to 60%'
principles.governmentExample: One pilot failure shouldn't abandon the approach; nor should one success prove it universally works. Both should proportionally update your confidence.

principles.description: Individual evidence should update from, not replace, prior probabilities
principles.badPattern: Ignoring base rates: 'This ministry succeeded, so all ministries can'
principles.goodPattern: Base rate anchored: 'Most ministries struggle with digital transformation; this success suggests good practices but doesn't change the overall difficulty'
principles.governmentExample: Even a successful DPI implementation shouldn't make you overconfident about replication - consider how often similar efforts typically succeed

principles.description: Not all variations in outcomes reflect meaningful patterns
principles.badPattern: Overreacting to noise: 'Usage dropped 5% this week, we need to change strategy'
principles.goodPattern: Noise-aware: 'Is this variation within normal range? Do we have enough data to conclude there's a real change?'
principles.governmentExample: Initial adoption numbers fluctuate; don't update your model based on early variations that might be random

principles.description: The evidence you see may be systematically biased
principles.badPattern: Ignoring selection: 'All the case studies show digital identity works'
principles.goodPattern: Selection-aware: 'Case studies are selected for success; what about the projects that failed quietly?'
principles.governmentExample: DPI success stories get published; failures get buried. Your evidence base is biased toward positive examples.

concepts.description: Your belief before seeing new evidence
concepts.example: Before the pilot, I was 60% confident this payment approach would work
concepts.application: Always start by articulating what you believed before the evidence

concepts.description: How much should this evidence update your belief?
factors: How surprising is this outcome if your model is right vs wrong?
How reliable is this evidence source?
concepts.example: The pilot succeeded, but it was a handpicked district with extra support - how much should this increase confidence about normal districts?

concepts.description: Your updated belief after considering evidence
concepts.example: After seeing pilot results, I'm now 75% confident (up from 60%), accounting for favorable pilot conditions
concepts.application: Explicitly state your updated belief and the reasoning for the update size

practicalTechnique.name: Pre-commitment and Review
steps: Before seeing results, write down your predictions and confidence levels
Identify what evidence would make you update up vs down
After seeing results, explicitly walk through the update
Document what changed and why for future reference
practicalTechnique.benefit: Prevents hindsight bias and makes updating deliberate rather than reactive

resistanceSources.description: Reluctance to update because you've invested in the old model
resistanceSources.symptom: Defending positions you've publicly committed to; protecting programs you championed
resistanceSources.override: Remember that updating now prevents larger future costs; your reputation benefits more from being right than from being consistent
resistanceSources.governmentContext: If a DPI approach isn't working, better to update now than defend a failing approach

resistanceSources.description: The model feels like part of who you are
resistanceSources.symptom: Taking evidence personally; feeling attacked when model is questioned
resistanceSources.override: Separate your identity from your models; being someone who updates is more valuable than being right initially
resistanceSources.governmentContext: Your value as an advisor comes from having good judgment, not from never changing your mind

resistanceSources.description: Others expect you to maintain your position
resistanceSources.symptom: Worrying about how changing your view will look; fear of being seen as inconsistent
resistanceSources.override: Frame updating as learning rather than flip-flopping; share the evidence that changed your mind
resistanceSources.governmentContext: Model updating as: 'Based on new evidence from the pilot, I've refined my thinking'

resistanceSources.description: Updating is cognitively effortful; easier to stick with current model
resistanceSources.symptom: Dismissing evidence as 'too complicated to process right now'
resistanceSources.override: Invest the effort for high-stakes decisions; create systems that make updating easier
resistanceSources.governmentContext: Build update discussions into regular review cycles so they become routine rather than exceptional

content.keyInsight: The goal is calibrated confidence - being exactly as confident as the evidence warrants, no more and no less. This requires both discipline to update when evidence supports it and discipline not to overreact to noisy or biased data.

exercises.prompt: Choose a key belief about DPI implementation (e.g., 'Biometric enrollment is feasible in rural areas'). Articulate your current confidence level and the evidence behind it. What evidence would move you up or down? Track how your confidence changes over the next month as you gather more information.

content.overview: Beyond fixing faulty models, you can proactively build better ones. This involves learning from experts, seeking diverse perspectives, and deliberately expanding your model toolkit. Better models lead to better predictions, decisions, and outcomes.

approaches.description: Systematically capture how experts think, not just what they conclude
approaches.technique: When consulting experts, ask 'How do you think about this?' not just 'What should we do?'
questions: What are the key variables you pay attention to?
What patterns have you seen across similar situations?
approaches.governmentApplication: When consulting DPI experts from other countries, extract their mental models, not just their solutions

approaches.description: Build models that recognize recurring patterns across contexts
approaches.technique: After multiple experiences, identify what they have in common
questions: What's similar about successful DPI implementations?
approaches.governmentApplication: After observing multiple ministry engagements, build models of 'what makes ministries receptive vs resistant'

approaches.description: Learn from others' experiences without bearing the cost yourself
approaches.technique: Study case studies and post-mortems with attention to model building
questions: What was their model going in?
What should I update based on their experience?
approaches.governmentApplication: Study DPI implementations in peer countries; extract model-relevant lessons

strategies.description: Each discipline has different mental models
strategies.application: For DPI, combine models from computer science (technical systems), economics (incentives), political science (power), sociology (adoption), and public administration (implementation)
strategies.benefit: Multi-disciplinary models catch what single-discipline models miss

strategies.description: Different roles see different aspects of the same situation
strategies.application: Include perspectives from frontline staff, managers, politicians, citizens, vendors - each has models built from different experiences
strategies.benefit: Reveals blind spots in your own role-based perspective

strategies.description: Actively seek out people who disagree with your model
strategies.application: Before committing to a DPI approach, genuinely engage critics and understand their counter-models
strategies.benefit: Forces you to confront evidence and arguments your model might dismiss

strategies.description: Assign someone to argue against your model
strategies.application: Before major decisions, have team members articulate how your model could be wrong
strategies.benefit: Surfaces weaknesses before reality exposes them

usefulModels.description: Every intervention creates responses that create new effects
usefulModels.application: When planning DPI intervention, ask: How will stakeholders respond? What will those responses cause?
usefulModels.example: Making digital permits mandatory (first-order) creates market for intermediaries (second-order) which may create new corruption points (third-order)

usefulModels.description: People respond to incentives; systems work when incentives align with goals
usefulModels.application: For any DPI component, ask: What incentives does this create? Are those incentives aligned with intended outcomes?
usefulModels.example: If ministry KPIs reward number of enrollments, quality might suffer; if they reward satisfaction scores, volume might lag

usefulModels.description: Systems are constrained by their limiting factor
usefulModels.application: Don't invest in components that aren't the bottleneck; identify and address the actual constraint
usefulModels.example: Building excellent enrollment software is wasted if the bottleneck is trained enrollment staff

usefulModels.description: Different populations adopt at different rates for different reasons
usefulModels.application: Early adopters need different support than late majority; what works for innovators may not work at scale
usefulModels.example: Successful pilot with tech-savvy citizens doesn't predict success with elderly rural population

usefulModels.description: Systems depend on trust relationships that must be deliberately built
usefulModels.application: Map trust requirements: Who needs to trust whom for this to work? How will that trust be established?
usefulModels.example: Digital ID adoption requires citizens to trust that their data won't be misused - what builds that trust?

content.keyInsight: Your mental models are tools. Like physical tools, you want a diverse toolkit and skill in choosing the right tool for each job. The best thinkers aren't those with one brilliant model but those with many adequate models and wisdom about which to apply.

exercises.prompt: Choose a recurring challenge in DPI work (e.g., ministry resistance, vendor management, citizen adoption). Build a mental model of this phenomenon: What are the key variables? What patterns have you observed? What does your model predict? Share with someone who has different experience and update based on their perspective.

content.overview: This final module guides you through a systematic audit of your own mental models. The goal is to identify which models are serving you well, which need updating, and how to build ongoing model maintenance into your practice.

auditProcess.description: List the domains where your mental models matter most
promptQuestions: What do you make decisions about?
What do you advise others about?
What do you predict or plan for?

auditProcess.description: For each domain, make your implicit model explicit
promptQuestions: How do you think this domain works?
What do you expect to happen when X changes?
auditProcess.technique: Write out your model as if explaining to someone who knows nothing about the domain

auditProcess.description: Understand where each model came from
promptQuestions: Is this from direct experience or received wisdom?
How old is the experience this is based on?
What context was it formed in?
auditProcess.warning: Models from a few vivid experiences may feel more certain than they should

auditProcess.description: Assess how well each model has served you
promptQuestions: When has this model predicted well?
When has it led you astray?
What surprises have you had in this domain?
What would others say about your judgment here?
auditProcess.technique: Be honest about failures; they're more informative than successes

prioritizationCriteria.description: How consequential are decisions in this domain?
prioritizationCriteria.priorityLogic: High-stakes domains deserve more model investment and scrutiny
prioritizationCriteria.governmentContext: Models affecting major DPI decisions need more attention than routine operational models

prioritizationCriteria.description: How confident are you in this model?
prioritizationCriteria.priorityLogic: Low-confidence models in high-stakes domains are top priority
prioritizationCriteria.governmentContext: If you're uncertain about political dynamics but they heavily affect outcomes, invest in better political models

prioritizationCriteria.description: How old is the evidence underlying this model?
prioritizationCriteria.priorityLogic: Models based on outdated information need refreshing
prioritizationCriteria.governmentContext: If your model of 'what technology can do' is from five years ago, it needs updating

prioritizationCriteria.description: How narrow is the viewpoint underlying this model?
prioritizationCriteria.priorityLogic: Models built from single-perspective need diversification
prioritizationCriteria.governmentContext: If your citizen adoption model is based only on urban, educated users, it needs rural/less-educated input

maintenancePractices.implementation: Quarterly: review key models and recent evidence. Annually: comprehensive audit
For major decisions, write down what you expect. After outcome, compare.
maintenancePractices.benefit: Creates objective data on model performance

maintenancePractices.description: Build relationships that challenge your models
maintenancePractices.implementation: Cultivate relationships with people who think differently; create safe spaces for disagreement

maintenancePractices.description: Treat surprises as learning opportunities rather than annoyances
maintenancePractices.implementation: When surprised, first ask 'What can I learn?' before 'What went wrong?'

commitments.meaning: Hold models lightly; be willing to be wrong
commitments.practice: Regularly say 'I might be wrong about this' and mean it

commitments.meaning: Update models even when uncomfortable or costly
commitments.practice: When evidence contradicts a cherished model, update anyway
Seek out information that might change your mind

commitments.meaning: Make your models explicit and open to critique
commitments.practice: Share your reasoning, not just your conclusions

content.keyInsight: Mental model maintenance is like physical fitness - it requires ongoing attention, not just a one-time effort. Build practices into your routines that keep your models fresh, tested, and aligned with reality.

exercises.prompt: Complete a personal mental model audit: (1) List 5 key domains where your models matter for your work. (2) For each, articulate your current model and its sources. (3) Identify which models are highest priority for updating. (4) Create a specific plan for how you'll improve and maintain your models going forward. Share this audit with a trusted colleague for feedback.

targetAudience: DPI advisors, government IT directors, policy coordinators working on digital transformation
